intent: Couple two bounded contexts symmetrically: each depends on the other, so neither may change its published interface without reaching mutual agreement.
problem: Two contexts need each other, so no upstream/downstream framing fits, but without an explicit relationship they negotiate ad hoc at release time — one team discovers a break caused by the other and the fix is whoever shouts loudest.
context: Partnership is the symmetric alternative to customer-supplier: mutual dependency, no upstream, no final word. Both teams must consult each other before changing a shared interface, which works when the collaboration is already well established, the teams are in frequent sync and continuous integration. Evans is explicit about the limitation: it is impractical across geographically distributed teams, and it becomes difficult when one team's priorities consistently override the other's — at that point the relationship is misdescribed and should be a partnership with explicit arbitration or, more honestly, a customer-supplier relationship with one side as supplier.
benefits: Changes that affect both contexts are agreed before they are made, not after they break.
Neither side's priorities are structurally subordinate, which keeps the model honest on both.
Integration decisions can be co-designed, so the boundary ends up in the right place.
No upstream model has to be adopted or translated — both models stay their own.
Cheap compared with a shared kernel, because the kernel is what really needs locking down.
tradeoffs: It requires continuous, frequent contact; geographic or organisational distance makes it impractical.
When one team consistently overrides the other, the partnership is a customer-supplier relationship in disguise.
Every interface change needs two teams in the room, which slows both down.
It is a relationship, not a mechanism: nothing enforces it, so it decays without attention.
Expensive to unwind — untangling a partnership is much harder than forming one.
quality_attributes_note: Nothing is mechanically improved; the gain is organisational (agreed interface changes), so the quality attributes are middling. reliability 7 from joint change agreement.

participants.responsibility: One side of the symmetric relationship; neither is upstream.
participants.notes: Each team may depend on the other for delivery.

participants.responsibility: The other side; equal standing, mutual veto on shared-interface changes.
participants.notes: Neither side has the final word.

participants.responsibility: The mechanism: frequent sync, continuous integration, agreed interface-change procedure.
participants.notes: Without this mechanism the pattern is just a label.

use_cases: Two product teams whose models genuinely interlock and ship together weekly.
Live Scoring and Event Operations, where a change in either is as important as a change in the other.
Two contexts inside one product team, split along model lines rather than team lines.
A pair of contexts where the overlap is large but neither is dominant.
avoid_when: The teams are geographically or organisationally distant — Evans calls this impractical.
One team consistently wins every argument; it is a supplier, not a partner.
The teams release on different cadences and neither can block the other.
The two contexts are actually independent and a thin integration would serve.
pitfalls: Calling a hierarchy a partnership because the labels are nicer.
A partnership with no forum, so changes get made unilaterally and argued about afterwards.
Assuming symmetry without checking the decision-making reality.
Letting the relationship quietly drift into a shared kernel, which needs more enforcement.
Never revisiting the boundary as the models evolve; the partnership outlives its purpose.

related_patterns_notes.shared-kernel: Partnership coordinates decisions; shared kernel coordinates a piece of model. Prefer shared kernel when the overlap is real but the coordination must be structural.
related_patterns_notes.customer-supplier: The asymmetric alternative; if one side has the final word, describe it honestly as customer-supplier.
related_patterns_notes.separate-ways: The deliberate opposite, for when coordination is impossible.

anti_patterns: A "partnership" where one team's roadmap is set unilaterally.
No mechanism — no shared integration pipeline, no regular forum, no change protocol.
Distributed teams paired without travel or shared working hours.
Using partnership to avoid making the hard call about which model is upstream.
design_principles: Partnership means two contexts succeed or fail together; the teams coordinate, with no upstream/downstream.
No team is allowed to change the public interface of the context without consulting the other and reaching mutual agreement.
Requires well-established collaboration, frequent sync and continuous integration; avoid across geographically distributed teams.
When both teams work on both contexts, the partnership relationship is much less costly (Graca).
Partnership is a symmetric relationship in the context map taxonomy.
best_practices: Build the mechanism before declaring the partnership: a joint integration pipeline and a regular interface forum.
Check the decision reality every few months; promote it to customer-supplier the moment one side wins consistently.
Keep the overlap small enough that agreement is cheap, or move to shared kernel where it is not.
Record the relationship and its forum on the context map so it survives staff turnover.
